plan.title: Mouse tumor immune/stromal deconvolution: anti-PD-1 vs isotype
plan.analytical_narrative: The question is cell composition, not differential expression: estimate the immune and stromal content of each of the 12 mouse subcutaneous tumors (6 anti-PD-1 vs 6 isotype control) and test whether it differs by treatment. The count matrix (12,000 mouse genes x 12 samples, Salmon-derived gene-level counts with unstated length correction) first passes sample-structure QC — mandatory because sample_01 has a library size ~4x below the median and its behavior must be inspected and reported, not silently dropped. Filtered, size-factor-normalized expression is then converted to the linear/log2 CPM input the deconvolution requires. Deconvolution uses mMCP-counter — the murine version of MCP-counter with marker sets derived from mouse data — because the knowledge service flags (R-0136) that human-profile methods (MCP-counter, xCell, EPIC, quanTIseq) are invalid on mouse tissue. The R-0136 premise that the mouse tool of record is absent does not hold in this environment: mMCPcounter 1.1.0 is installed in the R GitHub pool with its bundled murine marker set, so the deconvolution proceeds with it; a descriptive PanglaoDB (species=Mm) marker-score fallback via UCell is specified only if the murine feature set fails to load. Per-sample population scores are then compared between anti-PD-1 and isotype with exact rank-sum tests (n=6 per arm), BH-corrected, with effect sizes and a sample_01 sensitivity analysis. Composition is treated as the outcome (R-0132); no DE model is fitted because none was asked for. mMCP-counter scores are relative abundance proxies, not fractions or absolute counts — the report states this.

flags.message: If one sample has a library size several times below the median of the study, do not delete it in silence. Keep it through the sample structure QC, look at it on the PCA and on the sample distance heatmap, report its library size and its detected genes beside the others, and remove it only with a stated reason. The count models down-weight a low-depth sample through its size factor, thus removal is a judgment, not a default.

Do not run a human deconvolution method on mouse data. The marker sets and the reference profiles of MCP-counter, xCell, EPIC, and quanTIseq come from human samples, and a mouse symbol that maps to a human marker does not carry the same specificity in mouse tissue. The mouse tool of record is mMCP-counter, the mouse version of MCP-counter with markers from mouse data, and it is absent from this pool. Stop the deconvolution and ask for mMCP-counter or for a mouse reference, or give a descriptive signature score from mouse marker sets with the caution that it is not a deconvolution.
